extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of classical Euclidean solid geometry (readers of Euclid)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of Euclid Book XII solid-geometry propositions: theorems and constructions concerning cones, cylinders, spheres, and related polyhedra, with full proofs and constructive procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cone is one third of cylinder
rubrics_metrics.description: The cylinder is triple of the cone, or, the cone is the third part of the cylinder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by exhaustion/approximation: inscribe/circumscribe polygons in the circle base, erect pyramids on polygonal bases having the same vertex as the cone, compare volumes of pyramids and corresponding prisms/cylinders. By repeatedly subdividing the circle into polygons and comparing the contained pyramids to segments of the cone and cylinder, derive a contradiction if the cylinder were greater or less than three times the cone; thus the cylinder equals three times the cone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cones and cylinders of the same altitude are as their bases
rubrics_metrics.description: CONES and cylinders of the same altitude are to one another as their bases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If two cones/cylinders have equal altitudes, the ratio of the solids equals the ratio of their base circles. The proof uses inscribed/circumscribed polygonal approximations and comparisons of corresponding pyramids/prisms, showing impossibility of any other ratio by contradiction and subdivision into polygonal segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similar cones/cylinders scale by cube of diameters
rubrics_metrics.description: SIMILAR cones and cylinders have to one another the triplicate ratio of that which the diameters of their bases have.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If two cones/cylinders are similar, the ratio of their volumes is the cube (triplicate ratio) of the ratio of corresponding diameters (or homologous linear measures). The proof constructs corresponding similar pyramids filling the cones, shows each corresponding pyramid pair has the triplicate ratio of homologous sides, and extends to the whole cone; uses that each cone is one third of its cylinder to extend to cylinders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plane cutting cylinder parallel to bases
rubrics_metrics.description: IF a cylinder be cut by a plane parallel to its opposite planes, or bases; it divides the cylinder into two cylinders, one of which is to the other as the axis of the first to the axis of the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the cylinder generated by revolving a parallelogram about its axis. A plane parallel to the bases yields a circular section whose centre lies on the axis; the two resulting solids are cylinders whose volumes are proportional to their axes (altitudes). The proof uses taking equimultiples of the axes and comparing equal slices to deduce proportionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cones/cylinders on equal bases are as their altitudes
rubrics_metrics.description: CONES and cylinders upon equal bases are to one another as their altitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When bases are equal, the ratio of cones (or cylinders) equals the ratio of their altitudes. Proof reduces to cylinders first (cutting and comparing equal-base cylinders), then extends to cones using that a cylinder is triple its cone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bases and altitudes of equal solids are reciprocally proportional
rubrics_metrics.description: THE bases and altitudes of equal cones and cylinders are reciprocally proportional, and, if the bases and altitudes be reciprocally proportional, the cones and cylinders are equal to one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two directions: (1) If cones/cylinders are equal, then base1:base2 = altitude2:altitude1 — proved by comparing equal cylinders and cutting a cylinder to match altitude. (2) Conversely, if base and altitude ratios are reciprocal, construct subcylinders/subcones and use proportionality arguments to conclude equality. Proof handles both equal and unequal altitude cases by slicing with a plane parallel to the bases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polygon in larger circle not meeting smaller circle (construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: TO describe in the greater of two circles that have the same centre, a polygon of an even number of equal sides, that shall not meet the lesser circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: draw a diameter through the centre, draw a tangent from a point where diameter meets the smaller circle, repeatedly bisect arcs until a remaining arc small enough not to intersect the inner circle is found, erect equal chords around the great circle from that point to form an even-sided polygon whose sides do not meet the smaller circle; uses perpendiculars and properties of tangents and bisected arcs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma: radius comparison from trapeziums inscribed in circles
rubrics_metrics.description: If two trapeziums ABCD, EFGH are inscribed in circles with centres K and L respectively, with AB, DC parallel and EF, HG parallel, and AD, BC, EH, FG all equal, but AB greater than EF and DC greater than HG: then KA (radius of larger-circle trapezium) is greater than LE (radius of the other circle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction: assume KA ≤ LE and derive impossible equalities of circumferences by constructing an auxiliary circle with radius equal to KA about centre L and comparing arcs and straight-line lengths corresponding to equal chords; shows KA cannot be equal or less, hence must be greater. Corollary: analogous statement applies for an isosceles triangle with specified side/base relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polyhedron in larger sphere avoiding smaller sphere (construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: TO describe in the greater of two spheres which have the same centre, a solid polyhedron, the superficies of which shall not meet the lesser sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: cut both spheres by a plane through the centre producing concentric circles, on the larger circle apply the polygon construction from Prop. XVI to get an even-sided polygon not meeting the smaller circle, then erect pyramids (by joining polygon vertices to a point off the plane) and repeat symmetrically about diameters and hemispheres; assemble pyramids into a polyhedron inscribed in the larger sphere whose faces do not meet the inner sphere. Uses perpendicular planes, properties of great circles and equal semicircles to ensure faces lie outside the smaller sphere.
